newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FORECAST - Ringgit seen heading lower after budget.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Ringgit seen heading lower after budget.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit is expected to decline in the near term despite a national budget widely seen as currency-friendly, dealers and economists said at the weekend.
The ringgit would be pulled down by speculative selling after Friday's budget announcement, the strength of the U.S. dollar and a forecast of large monthly trade deficits for the rest of the year.
"It is a 'buy-on-rumour, sell-on-the-news situation'," said Jimmy Koh, economist with research firm I.D.E.A. in Singapore.
"Despite a bullish ringgit budget, players were unloading long ringgit positions," he said of trading immediately after the budget was announced.
Economists said the market had discounted budget expectations for the ringgit over the last few weeks.

They said a downward revision in the country's worrisome current account deficit in 1996 to 14.8 billion ringgit ($5.91 billion) from 17 billion, a steady trend in inflation and continuation of the tight monetary policy this year had already been built into the price.
"That is why the ringgit has retained its gains in the last few weeks despite dollar/yen being so strong," one dealer said.
Speculators have been accumulating the ringgit, one of the most actively traded currencies of the region, for the last month on budget expectations, foreign exchange dealers said.
Against a five-month low of 2.5110 a dollar on September 27, the ringgit moved up to 2.4980 in early October and eased slightly to trade in the 2.5020/70 range until budget day.
It has gained this year on the back of improving economic indicators, rising 2.45 percent against the U.S. unit from a low of 2.5680 a dollar on January 16.
Dealers and economists agreed that in the long-term, as the economy settled down to a sustainable eight percent growth rate, the ringgit would gradually gain against the U.S. dollar.
But, in the near-term it could be heading down to 2.52 a dollar due to year-end dollar demand in Malaysia, large monthly trade deficits and liquidation of long ringgit positions.

The Finance Ministry's Economic Report for 1996/97 forecast released ahead of the budget forecast the trade deficit at 5.2 billion ringgit for the year against 800 million for the first eight months and 9.2 billion ringgit in 1995.
The last quarter in Malaysia is usually the period when payment for large imports is completed and foreign firms repatriate profits, dealers and economists said.
Dealers said this would put pressure on the ringgit.
